abstract: Slow-wave sleep preserves the capacity for spontaneous or stimulus-evoked awakening despite reduced responsiveness, yet how thalamic nuclei coordinate to preserve arousability remains unclear. We analysed six fMRI and EEG datasets spanning sleep, propofol anesthesia and unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS). During N2 and N3, centromedian (CM) and ventral posterolateral (VPL) nuclei showed convergent edge-community profiles and increased closed-loop intra-thalamic motifs, changes not observed during anesthesia or UWS. During N3, directed effective connectivity along CM[->]VPL[->]pulvinar (PUL) increased versus wakefulness and N2. Stronger CM[->]VPL and VPL[->]PUL connectivity covaried with greater N3 delta power, which was higher before awakening than before transitions to N2 and positively associated with three-month improvement in behavioural responsiveness in UWS. These findings identify a CM-VPL-PUL-centred pattern of intra-thalamic organization linked to preserved arousability during slow-wave sleep, extending accounts focused on individual nuclei and thalamocortical interactions.
